stances.claim: Pre-EDSA PH party politics was an LP-NP 'duopoly' that, unlike US parties standing for opposing principles, 'did not essentially differ from each other in their political ideology and platform' -- existing 'mostly to perpetuate the political agenda of the party bosses who chose the party's candidates' -- making the parties nefarious and notorious enough that the 1987 Constitution discouraged the two-party system.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative-party-systems framing (PH duopoly vs US ideological parties)

stances.claim: The 1987 Constitution's party-list scheme -- 'borrowed from European parliamentary models and injected into our American-oriented presidential form of government' -- is an 'experiment' resulting in 'a political mongrel that, in all humility, I cannot comprehend fully,' making it one of CJ's strongest negative judgments on PH constitutional improvisation.

Under the 1987 Constitution, political parties play a minimal role in PRESIDENTIAL elections -- proven by 1992 (Ramos virtual-independent victory over LDP's Mitra despite Cory Aquino's LDP headship), 1998 (Estrada virtual-independent over Lakas-NUCD's De Venecia with Ramos's full support), with only 2004 as exception (Arroyo as incumbent candidate herself). Presidential candidates 'won on their personal charisma, not on the support of powerful political machines,' and Duterte and Poe (not backed by party in power) appear poised to continue this pattern in 2016.

Powerful parties retain some advantages -- election watcher appointment, election-return access (electronic precinct results + COC), allowable additional expenditures by supporting parties, ability to substitute deceased candidates -- and remain crucial for Senate elections (parties steering many senatorial bets to victory despite presidential loss) and provincial-level races.
stances.rhetorical_move: residual-relevance disclosure with specific advantage enumeration

stances.claim: Independents do not carry 'the baggage of discredited parties' and need not 'defend the shortcomings of incumbent presidents,' selecting their applauded projects/programs freely; meanwhile 'local dynasties thrive better under the present multiparty system' because limited national-party reach lets dynasties distribute local posts to favored members.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative-trade-off analysis (independent advantages + multiparty enabling dynasties)

notable_anecdotes: The pre-EDSA LP-NP characterization: 'They existed mostly to perpetuate the political agenda of the party bosses who chose the party's candidates, and by extension, the country's top officials' -- capturing why CJ characterizes them as 'nefarious and notorious.'

The 'political mongrel' epithet for party-list system: 'a confused and confusing party-list scheme, borrowed from European parliamentary models and injected into our American-oriented presidential form of government, an experiment which resulted in a political mongrel that, in all humility, I cannot comprehend fully' -- among CJ's harshest constitutional-mechanism characterizations.

The 1992 Ramos-Mitra paradox: 'Ramon Mitra, the candidate of the party in power (Laban ng Demokratikong Pilipino or LDP), miserably lost to a virtual independent, Fidel V. Ramos who, ironically, was backed by the LDP's titular head, President Cory Aquino.' -- historical irony preserved as evidence.

The 1998 De Venecia-Estrada parallel: 'Jose de Venecia who -- despite the full support of Ramos and the party in power -- also pitifully lost the 1998 presidential race to yet another virtual independent, Joseph Estrada.' -- using 'miserably' (1992) and 'pitifully' (1998) as parallel adverbs.
The 'baggage of discredited parties' metaphor -- using luggage imagery for unwanted political associations.

The closing dynastic-thriving observation: 'On the provincial level, locally-organized parties seem to be effective in propelling their candidates. In the same vein, local dynasties thrive better under the present multiparty system. Due to the limited reach of national parties, dynasties are able to distribute local posts to favored members.' -- connecting party-system design to dynasty entrenchment.

The Ramos-as-LDP-backed-virtual-independent + Estrada-as-PMP-founder pattern: presidents winning without party machines, then BUILDING parties to consolidate -- capturing the post-election sequencing.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban debunks the myth of powerful PH parties by contrasting them with their US counterparts. The US Democratic and Republican parties are 'slugging it out with full media coverage and unlimited spending' -- Clinton vs Sanders, Trump vs Cruz vs Kasich -- and stand for 'opposing principles and projects' with millions of members actively selecting candidates through primaries and caucuses that 'not even incumbent US presidents can dictate.' Pre-EDSA PH party politics, by contrast, was an LP-NP 'duopoly' briefly challenged by Manuel Manahan's Progressive Party (1957) and Raul Manglapus's Party for Philippine Progress (1965). The LP and NP 'did not essentially differ from each other in their political ideology and platform' -- existing 'mostly to perpetuate the political agenda of the party bosses who chose the party's candidates.' The two parties became 'nefarious and notorious' enough that the 1987 Constitution discouraged the two-party system and encouraged multiple parties; unfortunately, it also 'instituted a confused and confusing party-list scheme, borrowed from European parliamentary models and injected into our American-oriented presidential form of government, an experiment which resulted in a political mongrel that, in all humility, I cannot comprehend fully.' Under the 1987 Constitution, parties play a minimal role in PRESIDENTIAL elections. In 1992, the first race under the new Charter, Ramon Mitra (the LDP party-in-power candidate) 'miserably lost to a virtual independent, Fidel V. Ramos who, ironically, was backed by the LDP's titular head, President Cory Aquino.' Ramos formed the Lakas-NUCD to consolidate victory, which then backed Jose de Venecia -- who 'despite the full support of Ramos and the party in power -- also pitifully lost the 1998 presidential race to yet another virtual independent, Joseph Estrada,' who had founded Partido ng Masang Pilipino. Conventional logic says powerful parties propel presidential candidates to victory, 'but history has proven this to be a myth under the present Constitution' -- presidential candidates 'won on their personal charisma, not on the support of powerful political machines.' The only exception was 2004, with Arroyo as incumbent candidate herself. Will history repeat in May 2016 with leading candidates Duterte and Poe not backed by the party in power? 'In three weeks, we should definitely know.' Powerful parties retain some residual advantages: appointment of election watchers, entitlement to election returns and certificates of canvass, allowable additional expenditures by supporting parties, and substitution rights for deceased party-affiliated candidates (independents cannot be substituted). Parties remain crucial for the Senate, where they steer many senatorial bets to victory despite presidential losses. Independents 'do not carry the baggage of discredited parties and need not defend the shortcomings of incumbent presidents.' On the provincial level, locally-organized parties effectively propel candidates, and 'local dynasties thrive better under the present multiparty system. Due to the limited reach of national parties, dynasties are able to distribute local posts to favored members.'
